::: callout-note
## Scope

First-generation deconvolution fits a bulk profile with the **mean**
expression of each purified population. This review covers the methods
that also use the **distribution** of the purified profiles: at least
their variance, and in some cases a covariance between genes or
between cell types. DeCovarT belongs to that family: it plugs in a
gene–gene covariance per cell type and maximises a Gaussian-convolution
likelihood ([derivatives vignette](theory-decovart-generative-model.html#sec-unconstrained)).

Every method is read through the same lens: what its observation law
implies about the measurement process, most often UMI counts from
single cells. @sec-measurement states the measurement and expression
models that lens relies on, and @sec-eiv states the errors-in-variables
problem that every method solves. The methods follow, grouped by what
they estimate and what they assume known:

1. reference-based estimation of the composition, split by whether
   genes are treated as independent (@sec-methods);
2. cell-type-specific moments when the composition is known
   (@sec-cts-given-p);
3. Bayesian reference-based methods, for profiles or for proportions
   (@sec-bayesian);
4. semi-reference methods that infer one unknown component
   (@sec-semi-reference-methods);
5. reference-free methods that use co-expression structure
   (@sec-reference-free).

@sec-synthesis compares them and lists their caveats. The DeCovarT
model rebuilt for single-cell references is in the
[tailored vignette](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html).
:::

## Notation

Gene $g=1,\ldots,G$; cell type $j=1,\ldots,J$ (a second type is
$\ell$); bulk sample $i=1,\ldots,N$; reference donor (replicate)
$r=1,\ldots,R$; cell $c$, with $C_j$ cells of type $j$. Equations
quoted from a paper are translated into these indices; only
@tbl-notation-map keeps each paper's own symbols.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $y_{gi}$, $\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}$ | Bulk expression on a linear scale |
| $m_{ji}$, $n_i=\sum_jm_{ji}$ | Cells of type $j$ in bulk sample $i$, and their total |
| $\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i}=\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}/n_i$ | Bulk expression per cell |
| $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\in\Delta^{J-1}$ | Cell-number fractions, $p_{ji}=m_{ji}/n_i$ |
| $\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}$ | Transcript fractions, $q_{ji}=p_{ji}S_j/\sum_\ell p_{\ell i}S_\ell$ |
| $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=C_j^{-1}\sum_{c\in j}\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}=S_j\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$ | Per-cell mean of raw UMI counts of type $j$ |
| $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$, $S_j=\mathbf{1}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$ | Relative abundance ($\mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}=1$) and mean transcriptome size of a type-$j$ cell |
| $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ | Mean and $G\times G$ gene–gene covariance of a type-$j$ population profile (released DeCovarT) |
| $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j^{-1}$ | Precision of type $j$ |
| $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g$ | $J\times J$ covariance across cell types for gene $g$ (`bMIND`, `EPIC-unmix`, `Unico`) |
| $\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}$ | Purified profile of type $j$ in sample $i$ |
| $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}$ | Within-type cell-to-cell covariance (per cell) and between-replicate covariance of type $j$ |
| $a_i$ | Sample-wide scale |
| $x_{gc}$, $s_c$, $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}$ | UMI count, size factor, size-free expression of cell $c$ |
| $b_g$, $\tilde b_g=b_g^{\mathrm{bulk}}/b_g^{\mathrm{ref}}$ | Capture efficiency of one protocol, and the gene-wise platform ratio between bulk and reference; $\tilde{\boldsymbol{B}}=\operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}})$ |

A tilde marks a quantity rescaled to a reference unit: per cell
($\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}$, $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$) or relative to the
reference protocol ($\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$). Two kinds of covariance
are kept apart throughout: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ couples **genes**
within one cell type; $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g$ couples **cell types**
within one gene.
:::

# Measurement and expression models for single-cell counts {#sec-measurement}

A reference profile is a moment of a latent biological quantity, but
it is estimated from counts produced by a sampling protocol. Sarkar and
Stephens separate the two: a **measurement model** $p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\lambda})$
describes the protocol given the true expression, an **expression
model** $p(\boldsymbol{\lambda})$ describes the biology, and the
observation model $p(\boldsymbol{x})$ is their composition
[@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021]. Fang and Pachter add that
the cell-level scale factor is itself a product of a biological and a
technical term [@fangExtrinsicBiologicalStochasticity2025]. Both papers
index genes by $j$ and cells by $i$; below, gene is $g$ and cell is
$c$, so that $j$ remains the cell type.


## Poisson measurement of UMI counts {#sec-poisson-measurement}

If each molecule of cell $c$ is captured independently with a small
probability, the multivariate hypergeometric sampling of molecules is
close to a multinomial and each gene count is Poisson given the true
content (Supplementary Note 1 of
[@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021]):

$$
x_{gc}\mid s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c,m_{gc}
\sim\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c\,b_g\,m_{gc}\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c}=s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c\,\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}.
$$ {#eq-poisson-measurement}

Fang and Pachter write the same law as binomial thinning with capture
rate $b_gs^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$, of which the Poisson is the low-capture
limit, and normalise $\mathbb{E}[s^{\mathrm{bio}}]=\mathbb{E}[s^{\mathrm{tech}}]=1$
(their equations 1--2). Sarkar and Stephens instead take the observed
library size $x_{+c}$ as the size factor and a relative expression
$\lambda_{gc}=m_{gc}/m_{+c}$; in that convention $s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c$
cancels by construction, which is the removal of biological extrinsic
noise that Fang and Pachter warn about. The two conventions are the two
directions of the same rank-one Poisson fit: the point-mass MLE
$\hat\mu_g=\sum_cx_{gc}/\sum_cx_{+c}$ and the size-factor MLE of
@eq-poisson-size-factor below.

Three remarks connect the protocol to deconvolution.

- **UMIs remove most gene-specific distortion.** Unique molecular
  identifiers collapse PCR duplicates, which "substantially reduce
  unwanted variation, including differences in gene lengths and PCR
  amplification efficiencies" [@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021].
  What remains is a capture efficiency $b_g$ that is constant across
  cells of one protocol. It is not identified separately from
  $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$, and it cancels from every within-protocol
  contrast, so it is absorbed into $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$ and
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$. It does **not** cancel between a
  single-cell reference and a bulk library: the ratio
  $\tilde b_g=b_g^{\mathrm{bulk}}/b_g^{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the gene-wise platform
  factor of [plug-in scales (Strategy 4)](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-strategy-plugin). Read-count protocols without UMIs and
  hybridisation microarrays carry larger gene- and probe-specific
  factors (amplification, length, affinity), which is why earlier
  deconvolution methods had to model gene-wise scales explicitly; with
  UMI references, the gene-wise factor reduces to one cross-platform
  ratio per gene.
- **Random capture biases make the measurement overdispersed;
  constant ones do not.** If $b_{gc}$ varied from cell to cell, the
  measurement model would be negative binomial rather than Poisson
  (Box 1 and Supplementary Note 1.2 of Sarkar and Stephens). On spike-in
  controls the measurement dispersion was below $5\times10^{-3}$, which
  adds about 5% to the variance of a gene with ten observed molecules.
  Overdispersion seen in single-cell data is therefore an
  **expression** property, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j$, plus extrinsic
  noise, not a protocol property.
- **Zero inflation belongs to the expression model, if anywhere.**
  Spike-in controls show no zero-generating measurement component, and
  a point-Gamma expression model beats a Gamma model for only 0.6--8.6%
  of genes across the datasets tested
  [@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021]. Zeros are imperfect
  measurements of small $\lambda_{gc}$ at low depth, "with no need for
  special terminology or special treatment". For DeCovarT, which uses
  only the first two moments of the reference, a zero-inflated
  observation model is unnecessary: the moments of the counts already
  contain the zeros. The argument is made for UMI data; the authors note
  that it may not hold for read counts amplified by PCR without UMIs.

## Expression models and the observation models they induce {#sec-expression-models}

Integrating the expression model against @eq-poisson-measurement gives
the observation model gene by gene (Table 1 of
[@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021]).

| Expression model for $\lambda_{gc}$ | Observation model for $x_{gc}$ | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Point mass $\lambda_{gc}=\mu_g$ | Poisson | analytic |
| Gamma, mean $\mu_g$, variance $\mu_g^{2}\phi_g$ | Negative binomial | `edgeR`, `DESeq2`, `SAVER` |
| Point-Gamma | Zero-inflated negative binomial | `ZINB-WaVE` (multigene) |
| Unimodal or fully nonparametric | Flexible | `ashr`, `DESCEND` |
| Low rank, $\lambda_{gc}=\mu_{gc}u_{gc}$, $\mu=h^{-1}(\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{F}^{\top})$ | Flexible | GLM-PCA, `scVI` |

: Expression and observation models for UMI counts, after Sarkar and Stephens (Tables 1--2). The measurement model is Poisson throughout. {#tbl-expression-models}

A gene whose expression model is a point mass inside a homogeneous
population is a **Poisson gene**: its count has no variability beyond
sampling and the extrinsic size factor. Overdispersion relative to a
Poisson, the hallmark of the negative binomial, then measures either
biological variability of $\lambda_{gc}$ or variability of $s_c$.

## Extrinsic noise, size factors and Poisson genes {#sec-extrinsic-noise}

Fang and Pachter show that a cell-wide factor explains the baseline
overdispersion of single-cell counts. Under @eq-poisson-measurement with
$s_c=s^{\mathrm{bio}}_cs^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$ independent of
$\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}$, $\mathbb{E}[s_c]=1$ and
$\nu=\operatorname{CV}^{2}(s_c)$, their equation (3) reads, in our
notation and inside one cell type,

$$
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x_{gc},x_{hc})}{\mathbb{E}[x_{gc}]\mathbb{E}[x_{hc}]}
=\nu+(1+\nu)\frac{\Sigma^{\lambda}_{j,gh}}{\tilde\mu_{gj}\tilde\mu_{hj}}
+\frac{\delta_{gh}}{\mathbb{E}[x_{gc}]},
\qquad
1+\nu=(1+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}})(1+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}).
$$ {#eq-extrinsic-noise}

For two genes that are intrinsically uncorrelated, or for one gene that
is intrinsically Poisson, the normalised covariance equals $\nu$
(their equation 5). That identity gives an estimator of $\nu$ (the mode
of the normalised covariances over gene pairs) and a selection rule for
Poisson genes (those whose normalised variance minus the Poisson term
has a bootstrap interval containing $\hat\nu$). On those genes
$\mathcal{P}$, the size factor has the closed-form MLE

$$
\hat s_c=\frac{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{P}}x_{gc}}{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{P}}\tilde\mu_{gj}}.
$$ {#eq-poisson-size-factor}

Two findings matter here. Normalising each cell by its total removes
$s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c$ together with $s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$, and with it
the biological extrinsic variability, including cell size
[@fangExtrinsicBiologicalStochasticity2025]. In peripheral blood, sums
over Poisson genes no longer track total UMI counts and differ between
cell types, so the choice of size factor changes downstream
comparisons. Separating $s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$ from $s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c$
needs external controls (spike-ins, ambient RNA, pooled RNA); the
nascent-mRNA counts did not fit the binomial sampling model in their
pooled-RNA experiment.

## What the measurement model implies for the reference covariance {#sec-measurement-implications}

Write the same identity in matrix form (a direct consequence of
@eq-poisson-measurement and the law of total covariance; the
derivation is ours). With $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{b})$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}\mid c\in j)
=\underbrace{\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\bigr)}_{\text{Poisson measurement}}
+\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\Bigl[
\underbrace{(1+\nu)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j}_{\text{biology}}
+\underbrace{\nu\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}}_{\text{size factor}}
\Bigr]\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}.
$$ {#eq-count-covariance}

The sample covariance of raw UMI counts, which is what a single-cell
reference returns as $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}$, mixes three
objects. Only part of it belongs in the bulk law.

1. **The Poisson diagonal is single-cell measurement noise.** It is
   produced at single-cell depth and is not part of the tissue. A bulk
   library has its own sampling noise, on its own depth, which a
   diagonal bulk term would carry. Plugging raw-count
   covariances into $\boldsymbol{S}_W$ imports the reference sampling
   noise into the bulk covariance; subtracting $\operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j)$
   first removes it.
2. **The technical size-factor term is not biology either.** The
   rank-one term $\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}$
   induces a positive correlation between all genes. It inflates the
   apparent network and is a protocol artefact.
3. **The biological size factor is part of the bulk.** Cells of one
   type differ in volume and cycle phase; a tissue sums those cells as
   they are. The term $\nu^{\mathrm{bio}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}$
   belongs in $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$, and library-size normalisation
   that removes it understates the within-type variance that the bulk
   accumulates.

The corresponding moment estimator, with $\hat\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}$ from
spike-ins or Poisson genes, is

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}
=\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}_j-\operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j)
-\frac{\hat\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}}{1+\hat\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}}\,
\bigl[\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}_j-\operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j)+\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j^{\top}\bigr],
$$ {#eq-denoised-within}

where $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}_j$ is the sample covariance of the type-$j$
counts and $\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j$ their mean. It is the
$s^{\mathrm{tech}}$-free covariance of
$\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c}$ obtained by solving
@eq-count-covariance with $1+\nu=(1+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}})(1+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}})$
(our derivation, to be checked by simulation before use). Estimating
$\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}$ before the deconvolution is the first plug-in of
Strategy 4 ([plug-in scales (Strategy 4)](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-strategy-plugin)).

## Before single cells: measurement models for sorted population profiles {#sec-population-era}

Before droplet single-cell sequencing, a reference column was a bulk
measurement of a physically sorted population: FACS or magnetic sorting,
then a microarray or a bulk RNA-seq library. The measurement model was
the one of the platform, applied to a pool of many cells.

- **Microarrays.** A probe intensity is a background plus a
  probe-specific affinity times the abundance, with errors that are
  roughly additive at low intensity and multiplicative at high intensity.
  Analyses of differential expression worked on $\log_2$ intensities,
  where the multiplicative error becomes additive. Deconvolution could
  not: mixing is additive in the abundance, so the first reference-based
  methods fitted linear models on **unlogged** intensities
  [@abbasDeconvolutionBloodMicroarray2009; @shen-orrCellTypeSpecific2010; @lahdesmakiSilicoMicrodissectionMicroarray2005].
  The probe affinity is a gene-wise factor of the platform. It cancels
  within one platform and does not cancel between platforms, which is
  the origin of the gene-wise platform ratio $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ of later methods.
- **Bulk RNA-seq of sorted populations.** Reads are counts with a
  library size and a gene-length factor (for full-length protocols).
  Replicate libraries of one sorted population vary by a negative
  binomial dispersion that mixes biological and technical variation.
  Normalised counts on a linear scale (CPM, TPM) became the default
  input, with the same warning against logarithms.
- **What the reference variance meant.** With a handful of sorted
  replicates per population, the only second-order quantity available
  was a between-replicate variance of the population mean. That is the
  quadratic layer $\sum_jp_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}$ of the
  [tailored vignette](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-facs),
  and the object released DeCovarT was designed for. A within-type,
  cell-to-cell covariance did not exist in that design.

Two biases of sorted references have no single-cell analogue: sorting
selects cells on a few surface markers, so a "pure" population can
contain contaminating types; and the sorting itself can change
expression before lysis. Single-cell references remove the first by
labelling cells after the fact, and replace the platform model by the
Poisson measurement of @sec-poisson-measurement.

## From measurement models to bulk observation laws {#sec-observation-laws}

A deconvolution method chooses a law for the bulk. Read with the split
of @sec-measurement, that law is a measurement model (multinomial,
Poisson) composed with an expression model for the purified profiles
(Gaussian, log-normal, Gamma). @fig-observation-taxonomy places the
methods of this review by the support of $\boldsymbol{y}$ first.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-observation-taxonomy
%%| fig-cap: "Bulk observation laws of the reviewed methods, split by the support of the bulk (counts or continuous intensities), then by the law."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone"}}%%
flowchart TD
  A["Bulk observation law"] --> B["Discrete counts"]
  A --> C["Continuous intensities"]
  B --> D["Multinomial: ISOpureR, BayesPrism, gnSPADE"]
  B --> E["Poisson or Poisson-log-normal: DeconV, RCTD"]
  B --> NB["Negative binomial convolution: DeMixNB"]
  C --> F["Univariate Gaussian: DSection, BayICE, DWLS, MuSiC"]
  C --> RS["CLT Gaussian with noisy reference: RNA-Sieve, ReDeconv"]
  C --> LN["Log-normal components: DeMix, DeMixT, BLADE"]
  C --> G["Multivariate Gaussian convolution: DeCovarT"]
  C --> M["Moments only: DECALS, MEAD, CSNet"]
```

### Discrete counts {#sec-discrete-counts}

A multinomial (or Dirichlet–multinomial) model treats
$\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}$ as integer reads that sum to a library size.
`ISOpureR` implements a hierarchical multinomial–Dirichlet purification
of mixed tumour profiles [@anghelISOpureRImplementationComputational2015].
`BayesPrism` places a multinomial likelihood on bulk counts with a
patient-derived scRNA-seq prior and jointly infers $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$
and sample-level CTS expression [@chuCellTypeGeneExpression2022].
`DeconV` instead uses Poisson aggregation from single-cell to bulk
(sums of independent Poissons remain Poisson) and returns interval
estimates of $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$
[@gynterDeconvProbabilisticCellType2023].
`RCTD` is a Poisson–log-normal **mixture** of reads (@sec-rctd).

Over-dispersed, correlated counts are the domain of the multivariate
**Poisson–log-normal (PLN)** family: a latent Gaussian vector induces
dependence, and a Poisson observation layer yields integer reads
[@chiquetPoissonLognormalModelVersatile2021; @chiquetVariationalInferenceSparse2018].
**ZIPLN** adds a Bernoulli zero-inflation layer for dropout
[@batardiereZeroInflationMultivariatePoisson2025]. A DeCovarT-style
extension would replace @eq-gaussian-convolution by a PLN (or ZIPLN)
convolution on the latent log-abundance scale, keeping the ILR chart on
$\boldsymbol{p}$. A multinomial **logit-normal** on the *gene* simplex
is a different discrete model: it is compositional association, not a
cell-type convolution ([two simplices without convolution](theory-decovart-extensions-roadmap.html#sec-logit-normal-compositional)).

# Second-generation deconvolution: univariate versus multivariate {#sec-methods}

Second-generation methods use a single-cell reference and model, in
some form, the variability of the cell-type profiles. The usual split
into regression and probabilistic engines hides the property that
matters for DeCovarT: whether the bulk model treats **genes as
independent** (a diagonal variance per gene) or keeps a **gene--gene
covariance**. @fig-method-taxonomy uses that split.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-method-taxonomy
%%| fig-cap: "Deconvolution methods that model cell-type variability, split by their treatment of gene-gene dependence and then by estimator. All univariate methods assume independent genes; the multivariate ones differ by whether they commit to a density."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"curve": "basis"}}}%%
flowchart TD
  root["Variability of cell-type profiles in the bulk model"]
  root --> uni["Univariate: genes independent"]
  root --> multi["Multivariate: gene-gene covariance"]
  uni --> ureg["Weighted least squares"]
  uni --> ulik["Likelihood"]
  ureg --> music["MuSiC: cross-subject weights"]
  ureg --> dwls["DWLS: dampened relative-error weights"]
  ureg --> demixsc["deMixSC: fit-and-residual weights, platform-sensitive genes down-weighted"]
  ureg --> bisque["Bisque: gene-wise affine map, NNLS"]
  ulik --> sieve["RNA-Sieve: CLT Gaussian, noisy reference"]
  ulik --> rctd["RCTD: Poisson-log-normal mixture"]
  ulik --> redeconv["ReDeconv: variance-aware, CLTS"]
  multi --> mmom["Moment equations, no density"]
  multi --> mlik["Full Gaussian likelihood"]
  mmom --> decals["DECALS: subject-specific covariance, constrained OLS"]
  mmom --> mead["MEAD: errors in variables, dependency graph"]
  mlik --> deco["DeCovarT: convolution, sparse precision"]
```

## A common notation {#sec-notation-map}

Each paper uses its own indices; several use $j$ for the gene or the
subject. @tbl-notation-map maps them to this vignette. The scale
columns show how one model is reparametrised into another by
arithmetic alone.

| | This vignette | `MuSiC` | `RNA-Sieve` | `DWLS` | `deMixSC` | `Bisque` | `RCTD` | `DECALS` | `MEAD` | `Unico` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gene, type, sample | $g$, $j$, $i$ | $g$, $k$, $j$ | $g$, $k$, $b$ | $i$, $j$, -- | $g$, $k$, $j$ | $j$, $k$, $i$ | $j$, $k$, $i$ | $j$, $k$, $i$ | $g$, $k$, $i$ | $j$, $h$, $i$ |
| reference unit | replicate $r$ | subject $j$ | cell $i$ | cell | subject $j$ | individual $i'$ | cell | -- | individual $j$ | -- |
| target | $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ | $\mathbf{p}_j$ | $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ | $\mathbf{x}/\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{x}$ | $\mathbf{p}_j$ | $\mathbf{p}_i$ | $\boldsymbol{\beta}_i$ normalised | $\boldsymbol{\pi}_i$ | $\mathbf{p}_i$ | $\mathbf{Z}_{ij}$ ($\mathbf{w}_i$ given) |
| cell counts | $m_{ji}$, $n_i$ | $m_j^{k}$, $m_j$ | --, $n$ | $\mathbf{x}$ | $n^{k}_j$, $n_j$ | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| per-cell mean | $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=S_j\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$ | $S^{k}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k}$ | $\mathbf{M}_{\cdot k}$ | $\mathbf{S}_{\cdot j}$ | $r^{k}_{jg}=\theta^{k}_{jg}s^{k}_j$ | $\mathbf{Z}_{\cdot k}\approx\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$ | normalised mean | $\mathbf{w}_k$ (FPKM) | $\mathbf{U}_{\cdot k}$ | $\boldsymbol{\mu}_j$ |
| cell size | $S_j$ | $S^{k}$ (mean library size) | $\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{M}_{\cdot k}$ | assumed equal | $s^{k}_j$ | removed by CPM | removed | removed by FPKM | kept in $\mathbf{U}$ | -- |
| sample scale | $a_i$ | $C_j^{-1}$ | $n$ | $\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{x}$ | $n_j$ | -- | $N_ie^{\alpha_i}$ | absorbed | $\gamma_i$ | -- |
| gene platform | $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ | intercept $\alpha_{jg}$ | none | none | set $G_2$ down-weighted by $a$ | $(\beta_{0g},\beta_g)$ | $e^{\gamma_j}$ | none | $\lambda_g=\alpha_g/\alpha^{r}_g$ | none |
| type variability | $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g$ | $\sigma^{2}_{gk}$ (between, diagonal) | $s_{g,k}$ (within, diagonal) | -- | -- | -- | -- | $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{(k)}$ (between, full) | $\mathbf{V}_g$ (reference noise) | $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ ($J\times J$) |

: Notation of the reviewed methods mapped to this vignette. "Removed" means the normalisation divides each cell or column by its total, so that $S_j$ no longer enters the mean. {#tbl-notation-map}

Three reparametrisations recur.

- **Counts to fractions.** A model in cell counts,
  $\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i}$,
  becomes a model in fractions after division by the number of cells,
  $\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$.
  `RNA-Sieve` keeps $n_i$ as a parameter; `DWLS` estimates
  $\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i}$ (its "cell-type numbers") and normalises at
  the end.
- **Total molecules to average cell size.** `MuSiC` equation (2) gives
  $\sum_gX_{gi}=n_i\sum_jp_{ji}S_j$. Dividing by $n_i$ gives the average
  cell size of the sample, $\bar S_i=\sum_jp_{ji}S_j$, and `MuSiC`'s
  normalising constant is its inverse, $C_i=\bar S_i^{-1}$.
  Library-size normalisation therefore returns transcript fractions
  $q_{ji}=p_{ji}S_j/\bar S_i$, not cell fractions.
- **Scale times composition.** `MEAD` estimates
  $\boldsymbol{\beta}_i=a_i\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ and `RCTD`
  $p_{ji}e^{\alpha_i}$; both normalise at the end. The total of the
  unnormalised weights identifies the sample scale
  ([the sample-wide capture scale](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-cc-scale)).

## The common problem: errors in variables {#sec-eiv}

Every method of this review estimates a composition from two noisy
views of one latent truth: the purified profile
$\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}$ of each type in each sample. The bulk mixes
these profiles; the reference supplies only an estimate of their mean:

$$
\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}+\boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i},
\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}+\boldsymbol{v}_{\cdot j},
$$ {#eq-eiv}

with three mean-zero errors: the biological deviation
$\boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i}$ of sample $i$ from the type mean, the
measurement noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i$ of the bulk library, and the
estimation error $\boldsymbol{v}_{\cdot j}$ of a reference built from
finitely many cells or donors. Substituting the reference gives the
regression that every method fits,
$\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{e}_i$
with
$\boldsymbol{e}_i=\sum_jp_{ji}(\boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i}-\boldsymbol{v}_{\cdot j})+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i$:
an [errors-in-variables model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Errors-in-variables_model#Specification)
whose regressor is the reference. The methods differ by two choices.

- **Where the error is modelled.** $\boldsymbol{v}$ is an error in the
  regressor, the classical errors-in-variables layer; ignoring it biases
  $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ (attenuation, in the linear case) and
  understates its variance. `RNA-Sieve` models it in a joint likelihood
  and `MEAD` removes it with a bias-corrected estimating equation; every
  other method plugs $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ in as exact and models the
  response error $\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i$
  only.
- **How the error is specified.** (a) By a parametric law: Gaussian in
  DeCovarT, Poisson–log-normal in `RCTD`, Poisson in `DeconV`.
  (b) By an asymptotic law: the central limit over the $n_i$ cells of a
  sample, gene by gene, in `RNA-Sieve` and `ReDeconv`; the central limit
  over genes, $G\to\infty$, in `MEAD` and `DECALS`. (c) By its first two
  conditional moments only, $\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{e}_i\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})=\boldsymbol{0}$
  and a working $\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{e}_i\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})$,
  the route by which ordinary least squares is justified without a
  Gaussian assumption [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015, ch. 2].
  `DECALS` states this choice; `MuSiC`, `DWLS` and `deMixSC` make it
  implicitly through their gene weights.

The textbook assumptions do not hold here. The classical model takes the
errors independent of the true regressor and of each other, with a
constant variance
([terminology and assumptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Errors-in-variables_model#Terminology_and_assumptions)).
In DeCovarT the response error has covariance
$\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$, a function of the parameter; in
Poisson models (`RCTD`, `DeconV`) the variance equals the mean, again a
function of $\boldsymbol{p}$. Our reading: once the type mean is assigned
and the sample profile scatters around it independently of that mean,
the $\boldsymbol{u}$ layer is a
[Berkson error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Errors-in-variables_model#Berkson_errors),
which does not bias a linear estimator but enters weighted by the
coefficients $p_{ji}$, hence heteroscedastically. The $\boldsymbol{v}$
layer is classical, and DeCovarT ignores it by plugging in
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$, which is defensible only when every type has
many reference cells.

**Moment estimators give point estimates.** Weighted non-negative least
squares (`MuSiC`, `DWLS`, `deMixSC`) solves the normal equations
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})=\boldsymbol{0}$,
and `Unico` matches first and second sample moments explicitly. All are
[generalised method of moments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_method_of_moments)
estimators: consistent under correct moment conditions, but they return
a point estimate only. An interval needs more: a variance model with a
sandwich (`DECALS`), a likelihood (`RNA-Sieve`, DeCovarT) or a
resampling unit (genes, cells or donors). When the weights are
re-estimated from the residuals of the same fit (`MuSiC`, `deMixSC`), the
nominal weighted-least-squares covariance is not valid either (our
remark).

## Univariate methods: genes independent {#sec-univariate}

`MuSiC` starts from molecules: the bulk of subject $i$ holds
$X_{gi}=\sum_jm_{ji}S_j\theta_{gj}=\sum_jm_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}$, with
$S_j$ the mean total molecules per cell of type $j$ (equation 2). It works on relative
abundance $Y_{gi}=X_{gi}/\sum_{g'}X_{g'i}$, so that, with the
reparametrisation above,

$$
Y_{gi}=C_i\Bigl(\sum_jp_{ji}S_j\theta_{gj}+\varepsilon_{gi}\Bigr),
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_{gi}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})
=C_i^{2}\delta_{gi}^{2}+C_i^{2}\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}S_j^{2}\sigma^{2}_{gj}
=w_{gi}^{-1}
$$ {#eq-music-variance}

(equations 8--10). The second term comes from subject-level relative
profiles $\theta_{gj,i}\sim F(\theta_{gj},\sigma^{2}_{gj})$ (assumption
A1): it is the **diagonal** of the between-replicate layer
$\boldsymbol{S}_B(\boldsymbol{p})$, quadratic in $p_{ji}$, and it requires a
multi-subject reference. Cross terms between types are dropped, which
implicitly assumes independence across types. $\delta^{2}_{gi}$ is the
residual variance of the bulk. The within-type cell scatter
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ has no term in @eq-music-variance; it is
used only to select genes with small within-cluster variance in the
tree-guided recursion. Estimation is weighted non-negative least
squares, with the weights updated from an initial fit because
$\delta^{2}_{gi}$ is unknown, followed by rescaling to the simplex.

**Scales and identifiability.** $S_j$ is plugged in as the mean library
size of type $j$ in the reference. That substitution returns cell
fractions only under assumption A3$'$, a capture efficiency (observed
library size over molecule content) common to all types
([the `MuSiC` assumptions](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#fig-music-assumptions)); otherwise
`MuSiC` estimates the RNA-weighted product $p_{ji}S_j$. Under A1--A3
alone the paper claims only the trend of proportions across subjects.
Absolute $S_j$ is not needed: it cancels into $C_i$. A gene- and
subject-specific intercept $\alpha_{gi}$ absorbs protocol bias.
`MuSiC2` keeps the weights and removes genes that are differentially
expressed between the reference and bulk conditions
[@fanMusic2CellTypeDeconvolution2022].

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* response error only, specified by
two moments with a diagonal variance; $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ is
plugged in, and the estimator is a weighted moment estimator.

### RNA-Sieve {#sec-rnasieve}

```{.tikz}

%%| fig-cap: `RNA-Sieve` [@erdmann-phamLikelihoodbasedDeconvolutionBulk2021]. (a) With known per-cell moments $(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\boldsymbol{V})$, the bulk is the sum of $n_i$ cells drawn from the cell mixture, with a central-limit Gaussian per gene whose variance is the mixture variance. (b) The reference means are themselves noisy averages of $C_j$ cells; the joint likelihood over bulks and reference means is maximised, with Godambe sandwich intervals.
%%| filename: fig-dag-rnasieve
%%| alt: Two panels. Panel a: fixed per-cell means mu tilde and variances V outside a bulk plate; inside, fixed p_i gives the deterministic expected bulk per cell, mu tilde p_i, and the deterministic mixture variance sigma squared; with the fixed cell number n_i they generate the observed bulk y_i. Panel b: the same, plus an observed noisy reference mean generated by mu tilde, V and the fixed number of reference cells C_j.
\begin{tikzpicture}

\node[note, below=2mm of ya, align=center] (nya) {$y_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(n_i(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})_g,\ n_i\sigma^{2}_{gi}\bigr)$,\\ genes independent};
\plate{ia}{(etaa)(sa)(pa)(na)(ya)(nya)(nea)(nsa)}{$i=1,\ldots,N$}

\node[obs] (Mt) at ([xshift=-14mm, yshift=18mm]Mb) {$\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}$};
\node[const] (cj) at ([xshift=-16mm]Mt) {$C_j$};

\draw[edge] (Mb) -- (Mt); \draw[edge] (Vb) -- (Mt); \draw[edge] (cj) -- (Mt);
\node[note, below=2mm of yb, align=center] (nyb) {joint likelihood (10)--(11)\\ over $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$, $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$, $n_i$; Godambe intervals};
\plate{ib}{(etab)(sb)(pb)(nb)(yb)(nyb)(neb)(nsb)}{$i=1,\ldots,N$}
\node[ptitle] at (8.4,3.3) {(b) noisy reference, several bulks, eq. (9)--(11)};

```

`RNA-Sieve` writes the bulk as a sum of $n$ cells, each a draw from the
cell mixture [the mixture-of-cells covariance](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#eq-mixture-cell) restricted to one gene. By the central
limit theorem,

$$
y_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(n_i(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})_g,\ n_i\sigma^{2}_{gi}\bigr),
\qquad
\sigma^{2}_{gi}=\sum_jp_{ji}\bigl(V_{gj}+\tilde\mu_{gj}^{2}\bigr)-(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})_g^{2},
$$ {#eq-rnasieve-likelihood}

with genes independent (equations 5--8). The variance is **linear** in
$n_i$ and in $\boldsymbol{p}$, minus the square of the mixture mean: the
within-type variance $\sum_jp_{ji}V_{gj}$ plus the spread of the type
means, the diagonal of [the mixture-of-cells covariance](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#eq-mixture-cell). The reference means are noisy,
$\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\sim\mathcal{N}(\tilde\mu_{gj},V_{gj}/C_j)$ (equation 9),
and the true means are estimated jointly with $(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},n_i)$
from all bulks (equations 10--11). Marginalising them instead would add
$n_i^{2}\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}V_{gj}/C_j$ to the variance, a quadratic
term that vanishes as the reference grows (our remark).

**Scales.** Raw counts keep $S_j$ inside $\mathbf{M}$, so $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$
are cell fractions; the optional rescaling of every cell to the median
library size removes $S_j$ and turns them into RNA fractions. Any
global protocol difference is absorbed into $n_i$, which then "loses
interpretability" as a cell number across protocols (Supplementary S1.4). Intervals come
from the observed Fisher information or, by default, from the Godambe
matrix, centred at the Kullback--Leibler projection under
misspecification. The paper notes that gene correlation "may be
incorporated" once it is known, but does not implement it.

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* both layers; the response error has
an asymptotic (central-limit) law over cells, and the regressor error is
modelled in a joint likelihood.

### DWLS {#sec-dwls}

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-dag-dwls
%%| fig-cap: `DWLS` [@tsoucasAccurateEstimationCelltype2019]. The signature is the average of reference cells; the bulk is fitted in cell-type numbers $\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i}$ by iterated weighted least squares, with weights equal to the inverse squared fitted mean, capped by a dampening constant $w_{\max}$.
%%| filename: fig-dag-dwls
%%| alt: Observed reference cells inside a plate give the deterministic per-cell signature mu tilde hat. Inside a bulk plate, fixed cell numbers m_i and the signature generate the observed bulk y_i; a deterministic weight w_i, computed from the signature, m_i and the fixed dampening constant w max, enters the fit through a dashed arrow.
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[obs] (X) at (0,0) {$\boldsymbol{X}_{c}$};
\plate{cells}{(X)}{reference cells $c$}
\node[det] (mu) at (3.0,0) {$\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}$};
\node[note, above=1mm of mu] {cell averages};
\node[const] (d) at (6.0,0) {$w_{\max}$};
\node[note, above=1mm of d] {dampening};
\node[const] (m) at (1.8,-2.8) {$\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[det] (w) at (4.4,-2.8) {$\boldsymbol{w}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[obs] (y) at (3.0,-4.8) {$\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[note, below=2mm of y, align=center] (ny) {$w_{gi}=\min\bigl\{w_{\max},\ (\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i})^{-2}\bigr\}$ (rescaled), iterated WLS on $\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i}\ge 0$;\\ implied $\operatorname{Var}(y_{gi})\propto(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i})^{2}$, genes independent};
\draw[edge] (X) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (mu) -- (y); \draw[edge] (m) -- (y); \draw[edge] (mu) -- (w); \draw[edge] (m) -- (w); \draw[edge] (d) -- (w); \draw[dashededge] (w) -- (y);
\plate{i}{(m)(w)(y)(ny)}{$i=1,\ldots,N$}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

`DWLS` fits the cell-type numbers $\mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i}$ by

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{\cdot i}
=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{m}\ge\boldsymbol{0}}\sum_g\bar w_{gi}\bigl(y_{gi}-\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\boldsymbol{m}\bigr)^{2},
\qquad
\bar w_{gi}=\min\Bigl\{w_{\max},\ \frac{(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{\cdot i})^{-2}}{\min_{g'}(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g'\cdot}\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{\cdot i})^{-2}}\Bigr\},
$$ {#eq-dwls}

iterated from an ordinary least squares start, with $w_{\max}=2^{q}$
chosen to minimise the variance of estimates over random half-gene
subsets (equations 6--15). The purpose is stated on p. 7: with weights
$1/(\text{fitted expression})^{2}$ the loss becomes a function of the
relative error of each cell type, "because we would like all cell types
to be estimated with equal accuracy"; highly expressed genes, which
dominate an unweighted fit and favour abundant types, are down-weighted.
Read as a variance model, the weights imply
$\operatorname{Var}(y_{gi})\propto(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i})^{2}$,
a constant coefficient of variation, which the paper does not state.
There is no $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ term and genes are independent.
$\mathbf{x}$ are cell numbers only under equal RNA per cell; otherwise
they are RNA-weighted.

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* response error only, two moments with
a variance proportional to the squared mean; a weighted moment
estimator with no interval.

### deMixSC {#sec-demixsc}

<!-- TODO: add Guo et al. 2025 (deMixSC) to Zotero and replace the link by a citation key. -->
`deMixSC` keeps the weighted non-negative least squares of `MuSiC` and
`DWLS` and adds a small **benchmark** data set: bulk and single-nucleus
libraries prepared from the same nucleus aliquot, so that the real bulk
and the pseudo-bulk share the composition
([Guo et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.278822.123), p. 149). In
the 24 benchmark retinas, more than 5000 genes differ between the two
platforms in each batch, and TPM normalisation does not remove the
difference. In our notation the working model is (supplementary note,
equations S.1--S.5, pp. 1--2)

$$
y_{gi}=n_i\sum_jp_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}+\epsilon_{gi},
\qquad
\tilde\mu_{gj}=S_j\theta_{gj},
\qquad
\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}=\tilde\mu_{gj}+\bar\xi_{gj},
$$ {#eq-demixsc-model}

with mean-zero bulk noise $\epsilon_{gi}$ and an averaged single-cell
measurement error $\bar\xi_{gj}$. The residual of a fit with
$\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}$ is the estimation error plus a
"technological discrepancy" between platforms (note, p. 3). Two changes
to weighted NNLS follow.

- **Partitioned loss** (equation S.7, note p. 3). Genes differentially
  expressed between real bulk and pseudo-bulk in the benchmark form a
  set $G_2$ (5000 genes by default); their bulk value and reference are
  divided by a constant $a$ (1000 by default), which scales their
  squared residuals by $a^{-2}$:

  $$
  \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{p}\ge\boldsymbol{0}}
  \sum_{g\in G_1}w_{gi}\,r_{gi}(\boldsymbol{p})^{2}
  +\frac{1}{a^{2}}\sum_{g\in G_2}w_{gi}\,r_{gi}(\boldsymbol{p})^{2},
  \qquad
  r_{gi}(\boldsymbol{p})=y_{gi}-n_i\sum_jp_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}.
  $$ {#eq-demixsc-loss}

- **Weights** (equation S.9, note p. 3; main text p. 150):
  $w_{gi}^{-1}=\hat y_{gi}^{2}+(y_{gi}-\hat y_{gi})^{2}+c$, with
  $\hat y_{gi}=n_i\sum_j\hat p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}$ and $c=2$.
  Earlier methods, the authors note, use "either the squared fitted
  value" (`DWLS`, @eq-dwls) "or the variance" (`MuSiC`'s iteratively
  estimated $\delta^{2}_{gi}$, @eq-music-variance), "but never both"
  (p. 157). The fit is iterated from an NNLS start (note, p. 4).

The target cohort is first aligned to the benchmark bulk by quantile
normalisation and `ComBat` (p. 150). The platform effect is treated as
noise to down-weight, not as a gene-wise ratio $\tilde b_g$ to estimate:
with $a=1000$ the genes of $G_2$ receive a weight $10^{-6}$ times
smaller, which nearly discards them. The squared residual in the weight
uses one residual per gene as its own variance, an outlier-damping
device in the spirit of robust M-estimation rather than a variance
model (our reading). Cell size enters through
$\tilde\mu_{gj}=S_j\theta_{gj}$, as in `MuSiC`, so $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$
are cell fractions under the same equal-efficiency assumption. No
interval is reported.

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* both layers are written down but enter
only through the weights; a weighted moment estimator with no interval.

### Bisque {#sec-bisque}

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-dag-bisque
%%| fig-cap: `Bisque` [@jewAccurateEstimationCell2020], paired mode. For individuals with both assays, the single-cell counts give a CPM signature $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and counted proportions, hence a pseudo-bulk; a gene-wise linear map from observed bulk to pseudo-bulk is learned on those pairs and applied to the remaining bulks before non-negative least squares.
%%| filename: fig-dag-bisque
%%| alt: A plate over paired individuals contains observed cells, the deterministic counted proportions p_i' and the deterministic pseudo-bulk y ps_i' = theta p_i', and the observed paired bulk. The deterministic CPM signature theta is computed from the cells. A deterministic gene-wise map beta_0, beta is learned from pseudo-bulk and paired bulk. Inside a bulk plate, the map, theta and the fixed proportions p_i generate the observed bulk y_i.
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[obs] (Xc) at (0,0) {$\boldsymbol{X}_{c}$};

\node[det] (pp) at (2.2,0) {$\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i'}$};
\node[det] (eta) at (2.2,-2.0) {$\boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{ps}}_{\cdot i'}$};
\node[obs] (yp) at (4.2,-2.0) {$\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i'}$};
\node[note, below=1mm of eta] (neta) {$\boldsymbol{\theta}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i'}$};
\plate{ip}{(cells)(cells-lab)(pp)(eta)(yp)(neta)}{paired individuals $i'$}
\node[det] (Z) at (-0.6,-4.2) {$\boldsymbol{\theta}$};

\node[note, below=2mm of y, align=center] (ny) {$\beta_{0g}+\beta_g y_{gi}=(\boldsymbol{\theta}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})_g+e_{gi}$;\\ NNLS with sum to one};
\draw[edge] (Xc) -- (pp); \draw[edge] (Xc) to[out=-120, in=110] (Z); \draw[edge] (Z) -- (eta); \draw[edge] (pp) -- (eta);
\draw[edge] (eta) to[bend left=35] (beta); \draw[edge] (yp) -- (beta);
\draw[edge] (beta) -- (y); \draw[edge] (p) -- (y); \draw[edge] (Z) -- (y);
\plate{i}{(p)(y)(ny)}{$i=1,\ldots,N$}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

`Bisque` learns the platform shift instead of modelling it. In paired
mode it fits $y^{\mathrm{ps}}_{gi'}=\beta_{0g}+\beta_gy_{gi'}+\epsilon_{gi'}$ per
gene, with $\boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{ps}}_{\cdot i'}=\boldsymbol{\theta}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i'}$
the pseudo-bulk of individual $i'$ (equation 1); in unpaired mode it
matches the first two moments of each gene across samples (equations
2--3). The transformed bulk is then fitted by non-negative least squares
with a sum-to-one constraint. The fitting step has homoscedastic
residuals; the variability of the reference enters only through the
between-sample moments used in the map. Because $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is
built from CPM, cell size is removed from the signature; the gene-wise
affine map absorbs the platform ratio $\tilde b_g$ (as $1/\beta_g$) and
an intercept, not a type-specific $S_j$. In unpaired mode the cohort
mean composition is assumed equal to the mean composition of the
single-cell individuals.

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* the platform error is removed by a
learned map, then a homoscedastic moment estimator; no interval.

### RCTD {#sec-rctd}

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-dag-rctd
%%| fig-cap: `RCTD` [@cableRobustDecompositionCell2022a] in this vignette's notation. The reference is collapsed to fixed normalised means $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\cdot j}$. Sample $i$ carries an observed depth $L_i$, a leftover scale $\alpha_i$, a composition and a gene-wise overdispersion; the platform ratio $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ is shared across samples and is not estimated inside the per-sample fit.
%%| filename: fig-dag-rctd
%%| alt: Observed reference cells give the deterministic normalised means theta hat. A fixed platform ratio b tilde sits outside the sample plate. Inside the plate, the observed depth L_i, the fixed scale alpha_i, the fixed composition p_i and the latent overdispersion epsilon_i combine with theta hat and b tilde into the deterministic rate lambda_i, which with L_i generates the observed counts y_i through a Poisson law.
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[obs] (Xc) at (0,0) {$\boldsymbol{X}_{c}$};
\plate{cells}{(Xc)}{reference cells}
\node[det] (mu) at (2.8,0) {$\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\cdot j}$};
\node[note, above=1mm of mu] {normalised means};
\node[const] (d) at (5.0,0) {$\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$};
\node[note, above=1mm of d] {platform};
\node[obs] (N) at (-0.4,-2.6) {$L_i$};
\node[const] (al) at (1.2,-2.6) {$\alpha_i$};
\node[const] (p) at (2.8,-2.6) {$\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[stoch] (e) at (4.6,-2.6) {$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[det] (lam) at (2.4,-4.4) {$\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[obs] (y) at (2.4,-6.2) {$\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[note, right=2mm of lam, align=left] (nl) {$\log\lambda_{gi}=\alpha_i+\log\bigl(\sum_j p_{ji}\hat\theta_{gj}\bigr)$\\ $\quad+\log\tilde b_g+\varepsilon_{gi}$};
\node[note, right=2mm of y] (ny) {$y_{gi}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(L_i\lambda_{gi})$};
\draw[edge] (Xc) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (mu) -- (lam); \draw[edge] (d) -- (lam);
\draw[edge] (al) -- (lam); \draw[edge] (p) -- (lam); \draw[edge] (e) -- (lam);
\draw[edge] (lam) -- (y); \draw[edge] (N) |- (y);
\plate{i}{(N)(al)(p)(e)(lam)(y)(nl)(ny)}{$i=1,\ldots,N$}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

`RCTD` works one layer below DeCovarT. Each UMI first picks a type with
probability $p_{ji}$, then a gene from that type's relative profile: a
read-level **mixture**, not a convolution of random population profiles
[@cableRobustDecompositionCell2022a]. Given the rate, gene counts are
Poisson; the rate is log-normal around a linear mixture of the **fixed**
normalised means $\theta_{gj}$ (supplementary equations 3, 22):

$$
y_{gi}\mid\lambda_{gi}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(L_i\lambda_{gi}),
\qquad
\log\lambda_{gi}=\alpha_i+\log\Bigl(\sum_jp_{ji}\theta_{gj}\Bigr)+\gamma_g+\varepsilon_{gi},
$$ {#eq-rctd-pln}

with $L_i$ the observed depth, $\alpha_i$ a leftover sample scale,
$\gamma_g$ the platform effect and $\varepsilon_{gi}$ an independent,
heavy-tailed $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2)$ overdispersion. The
Poisson mean is

$$
\mathbb{E}[y_{gi}\mid\varepsilon_{gi}]
=\underbrace{L_ie^{\alpha_i}}_{a_i}\,\tilde b_g\,e^{\varepsilon_{gi}}\sum_jp_{ji}\theta_{gj},
\qquad
\tilde b_g=e^{\gamma_g},
$$ {#eq-rctd-mean}

so the platform effect is exactly the gene-wise ratio $\tilde b_g$ of
@sec-poisson-measurement, and $\varepsilon_{gi}$ is the count-scale
analogue of a diagonal bulk residual. Genes are independent given
$\varepsilon$. In the language of the measurement model, the rate of
gene $g$ is a type-weighted sum of per-type rates scaled by one
sample-wide factor; the same holds in DeCovarT's single-cell mean
$a_in_i\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$, whose
per-type contribution is $n_ip_{ji}S_j$ molecules of profile
$\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$ (our reading). A mixture is the right
story at the UMI; a convolution of random profiles
(@eq-gaussian-convolution) is the right story for population profiles.

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-rctd-two-stage
%%| fig-cap: `RCTD` estimation. Stage 1 identifies the gene-wise platform ratio from a pseudobulk of all samples; stage 2 fits each sample by sequential quadratic programming on the unnormalised weights $w_{ji}=p_{ji}e^{\alpha_i}$.
%%| filename: fig-rctd-two-stage
%%| alt: Flowchart. Library-normalised cells are averaged to theta hat; differentially expressed genes are kept; together with a pseudobulk of all samples they enter stage 1, a maximum-likelihood fit of the platform ratio b tilde and a bulk-wide mixture. The estimates are plugged into the Poisson-log-normal model; stage 2 runs a per-sample SQP on non-negative weights, which are normalised to give p hat.
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.append style={text width=3.4cm}]
\node[box] (avg) at (0,0) {average library-normalised cells to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\cdot j}$};
\node[box] (filt) at (0,-1.7) {keep differentially expressed genes};
\node[box] (pool) at (4.4,-1.7) {pool all samples into one pseudobulk};
\node[keybox] (s1) at (2.2,-3.6) {Stage 1: MLE of platform $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ and a bulk-wide mixture};
\node[box] (plug) at (2.2,-5.3) {plug $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\cdot j}$ and $\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}}$ into the Poisson--log-normal};
\node[keybox] (s2) at (2.2,-7.0) {Stage 2: per-sample SQP on $w_{ji}=p_{ji}e^{\alpha_i}\ge 0$};
\node[box] (rec) at (2.2,-8.7) {$\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}=\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_{\cdot i}/\mathbf{1}^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_{\cdot i}$};
\draw[edge] (avg) -- (filt); \draw[edge] (filt) -- (s1); \draw[edge] (pool) -- (s1);
\draw[edge] (s1) -- (plug); \draw[edge] (plug) -- (s2); \draw[edge] (s2) -- (rec);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

The fit is two-stage because $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ cannot be free
inside one sample ([alignment scales](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-alignment)):
stage 1 estimates $\gamma_g$ from one pseudobulk of all spots
(supplementary equations 14--19), stage 2 holds it fixed. That is
Strategy 4 in its purest form ([plug-in scales](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-strategy-plugin)).
Stage 2 maximises a non-convex Poisson–log-normal likelihood in
$w_{ji}=p_{ji}e^{\alpha_i}\ge0$ by sequential quadratic programming: the
Hessian is replaced by its positive-semidefinite part and each step is a
constrained quadratic programme with step size $0.3$. Zeros on the
orthant boundary are native to that formulation, which suits spots with
few types. DeCovarT instead maps $\boldsymbol{p}$ to the ILR chart and
takes Newton–Raphson steps with the analytic score and Hessian of a
Gaussian law.

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* response error only, with a parametric
(Poisson–log-normal) law; the reference means are plugged in and the
platform ratio is a plug-in from stage 1.

### ReDeconv {#sec-redeconv}

`ReDeconv` names three ways a single-cell reference distorts
deconvolution: rescaling every cell to a common total (CP10K), which
erases transcriptome size; the gene-length mismatch between UMI
single-cell counts and full-length bulk libraries; and ignoring the
within-type variance [@luTranscriptomeSizeMatters2025].

**Model.** The bulk is a sum of $m_{ji}$ independent cells of each
type. By the central limit theorem, after a rescaling of the bulk by a
constant $c$ and with weights $f_{ji}=cm_{ji}$,

$$
y_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}\Bigl(\sum_jf_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj},\ c\sum_jf_{ji}\sigma^{2}_{gj}\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-redeconv}

with genes independent, and the composition is estimated by maximising
the product of these densities over genes. The variance is **linear**
in the weights, the diagonal of the within-type layer
$n_i^{-1}\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$
([one replicate](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-one-replicate)),
as in `RNA-Sieve` without the spread of type means. The optimiser, the
estimation of $c$ and the final simplex step are not stated.

**Transcriptome size.** CLTS normalisation fits, for each single-cell
sample $r$, a line $S_{jr}=\alpha_rS_{j1}+\beta_r$ between its mean
transcriptome sizes per type and those of a baseline sample, then
rescales every count of sample $r$ as
$x_{gc}\leftarrow x_{gc}/\alpha_r+(v_{\max}-\beta_r/\alpha_r)/G$ with
$v_{\max}=\max_r\beta_r/\alpha_r$. Differences of transcriptome size
between types within a sample are kept; differences between samples are
removed. CLTS therefore keeps $S_j$ in
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=S_j\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}$, so
the fitted weights are cell fractions rather than transcript fractions.

**Caveats.** About 100 signature genes per type are chosen by a $t$-test,
a fold change and a small coefficient of variation; the synthetic
benchmarks draw bulk and reference from the same single-cell source, as
the authors acknowledge.

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* response error only, with an
asymptotic (central-limit) law over cells; the reference is plugged in.

## Multivariate methods: gene--gene covariance {#sec-multivariate}

### DECALS {#sec-decals}

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-dag-decals

(b) Constrained generalised least squares when $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ is known. (c) `DECALS` proper: the type covariances are unknown and are estimated from bulk residuals across samples, with a bias correction iterated with the variance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}$; the point estimate stays the OLS one.

```

`DECALS` makes no distributional assumption on the bulk. Its model
(equations 1--2, 5) is

$$
\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}_i
=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i)=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j,
$$ {#eq-decals-model}

with subject-level type profiles $\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}_i$ independent
across types: exactly the quadratic layer $\boldsymbol{S}_B(\boldsymbol{p})$
and released DeCovarT's covariance, without a density. The three panels
of @fig-dag-decals are the paper's three estimators.

1. **Constrained OLS** (equation 3) is the point estimator. For a large
   number of genes the inequality constraints are inactive and the
   estimator is the equality-constrained projection
   $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}=\mathbf{U}\tilde{\boldsymbol{p}}$ of the OLS solution
   (Lemma S1). Its asymptotic covariance is the sandwich
   $\boldsymbol{V}_i=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{U}^{\top}$ with
   $\mathbf{D}=(\tfrac1G\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu})^{-1}\tfrac1G\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\boldsymbol{\mu}(\tfrac1G\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu})^{-1}$.
2. **Constrained GLS** with known $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i$ (equations 10--11)
   is more efficient. The authors reject it once $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i$ is
   estimated: the per-sample inverse square root is too noisy, and the
   coverage of GLS with an estimated covariance falls to about 0.65--0.8
   in their simulations.
3. **Unknown $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$.** Because
   $\mathbb{E}[z_{gi}z_{hi}]=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\Sigma_{j,gh}$, the
   residual outer products are regressed on the squared proportions
   across the $N$ samples, $\hat{\boldsymbol{c}}_{gh}=(\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{H}})^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}(\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_g\circ\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_h)$
   with $\hat{\mathbf{H}}=[\hat p_{ji}^{2}]$ (equation 6), a regression
   first proposed for known proportions by CSNet. Replacing
   $\mathbf{H}$ by $\hat{\mathbf{H}}$ deflates the estimate; Proposition 1
   gives the bias terms $\mathbf{B}_1,\mathbf{B}_2$ under a Gaussian
   approximation of $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$, and the corrected estimator
   (equation 7) is iterated with $\boldsymbol{V}_i$, then thresholded by
   SCAD and projected onto the positive semidefinite cone.

**Asymptotics.** Genes are the statistical units: Theorem 1 gives
$\sqrt{G}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\to\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{V}_i)$
as $G\to\infty$ for one sample, under sub-exponential errors, a
dependency graph of bounded degree among genes, and
$p_{ji}>0$ for all types. On a face of the simplex the limit law is not
derived. With dense gene correlation the authors report that coverage
collapses to about 0.65: the central limit theorem over genes fails
when dependence is not sparse. The paper gives no consistency theorem
for $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j$.

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* response error only, specified by two
moments with the composition-dependent covariance of DeCovarT; an
asymptotic law over genes yields the sandwich interval.

`MEAD` is the multivariate errors-in-variables method. Its successive
models (@fig-dag-mead), translated into our indices, are:

- **Scales** (equations 2--3). The bulk is
  $\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=a_i\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{b}^{\mathrm{bulk}})\mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i$
  and reference individual $r$ is
  $\mathbf{Z}_r=a^{\mathrm{ref}}_r\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{b}^{\mathrm{ref}})\mathbf{X}^{\mathrm{ref}}_r+\mathbf{E}_r$,
  with $\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\mathbf{X}^{\mathrm{ref}}_r$ drawn from one
  population law (assumption 1). $a_i$ captures depth and tissue
  amount, $\boldsymbol{b}$ gene length and GC content. The reference
  scale is one scalar per reference individual, shared by its cell
  types (Supplementary S2.1); the authors avoid per-cell library-size
  normalisation to keep cell size in $\boldsymbol{\mu}$.
- **Reparametrisation** (equations 4--5). Only the ratio
  $\tilde b_g=b^{\mathrm{bulk}}_g/b^{\mathrm{ref}}_g$ is identified, and
  assumption 3 treats it as noise,
  $\tilde b_g\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}[1,\sigma_0^{2}]$, independent of
  $\boldsymbol{\mu}$. The model becomes
  $\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\beta}_i+\boldsymbol{e}_i$
  with $\boldsymbol{\beta}_i=a_i\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ and
  $\boldsymbol{e}_i=(\tilde{\boldsymbol{B}}-\mathbf{I})\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\beta}_i+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}'_i$:
  the platform ratio is not estimated, inflates the variance and makes
  $\boldsymbol{e}_i$ dependent across samples.
- **One sample.** With $\hat a^{\mathrm{ref}}_r=\sum_{j,g}z_{rgj}/(JG)$
  (a plug-in from the reference alone), $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{g\cdot}$ the
  average of $\boldsymbol{z}_{rg\cdot}/\hat a^{\mathrm{ref}}_r$ and
  $\hat{\mathbf{V}}_g$ its covariance across reference individuals, the
  bias-corrected estimating equation

  $$
  \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}-\bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\hat{\mathbf{V}}\bigr)\boldsymbol{\beta}_i=\boldsymbol{0},
  \qquad
  \hat{\mathbf{V}}=\sum_gw_g\hat{\mathbf{V}}_g,
  $$ {#eq-mead-estimating}

  removes the attenuation caused by a noisy regressor (equation 6).
  Non-negativity is imposed by truncation or constrained optimisation,
  and $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_i/\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_i\|_1$.
- **Several samples** (section 5). The composition is regressed on
  covariates, $\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}]=h(\boldsymbol{b}_0+\mathbf{A}_0^{\top}\boldsymbol{f}_i)$,
  with $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}$ plugged into an estimating
  equation (11).
- **Dependence and weights.** Gene–gene dependence is global, not type
  specific: a dependency graph over genes, estimated from the bulk
  correlation by a multiple test, enters only the sandwich covariance.
  The weights $w_g=1/\tilde s_g^{2}$, with
  $s_g^{2}=\mathbf{1}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{V}}_g\mathbf{1}$ shrunk across
  genes, come from the reference only; `MuSiC`'s residual-based weights
  "can severely bias" the estimating equation.

**Identifiability** (Theorem 1). With a composition matrix of rank $J$,
the proportions are identifiable if and only if $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ has
full rank and, for every partition of the genes into $t\ge2$ blocks,
the ranks of the blocks of $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ add to more than $J$.
**Perfect marker genes** violate the condition: rescaling the
platform ratios of the type-$j$ markers by $1/\delta_j$, the
proportions to $\tilde p_{ji}=\delta_jp_{ji}/\sum_\ell\delta_\ell p_{\ell i}$
and the scale to $a_i\sum_\ell\delta_\ell p_{\ell i}$ leaves the bulk
mean unchanged, for any $\boldsymbol{\delta}$. A gene-wise platform
ratio can then mimic a type-specific size factor (Supplementary Remark
S1), the $\boldsymbol{q}$ versus $\boldsymbol{p}$ ambiguity of
[alignment scales](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-alignment);
assumption 3 restores identification because a ratio that depends on
the type of its marker is no longer independent of $\boldsymbol{\mu}$
(our reading).

**Asymptotics.** With $G\to\infty$ and the number of reference
individuals fixed, Theorems 2--3 give
$\sqrt{G}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\to\mathcal{N}\bigl(\boldsymbol{0},\nabla g\,\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}^{-1}\nabla g^{\top}\bigr)$,
with the Gram limit
$\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}=\lim G^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\mu}$,
when every $p_{ji}>0$ and the dependency graph is "almost sparse". The
regime is fragile when the reference-noise term does not shrink (fixed
number of reference individuals), when types are collinear, at the
boundary (the softplus device is inconsistent for finite tuning), and
for the composition regression unless $N=o(G)$ (Theorem 4, Remark S3).
`DECALS` reports that `MEAD` underestimates variances.

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* both layers; the regressor error is
removed by a bias-corrected estimating equation and the platform ratio
is a multiplicative response error; the law is asymptotic in $G$.

## Where DeCovarT sits {#sec-decovart-dag}

Released DeCovarT plugs in the mean and gene–gene covariance of each
type and fits the Gaussian convolution of @eq-gaussian-convolution, one
bulk sample at a time. Against the methods above:

- `RNA-Sieve` and `ReDeconv` sum independent **cells**, so a type's
  variance enters linearly in $p_{ji}$, gene by gene; DeCovarT convolves
  random **population profiles**, so it enters quadratically and keeps
  the gene–gene covariance.
- `DECALS` assumes the same covariance, $\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$,
  without a density; its point estimate is least squares and its
  efficiency depends on how well the covariance is estimated across
  bulks. `MEAD` keeps a global gene dependence and adds the platform
  ratio, but models the reference noise that DeCovarT ignores.
- `RCTD` is a read-level mixture with gene-wise overdispersion, not a
  type-level covariance.

For a single-cell reference the bulk is a physical sum of cells, and
the variance becomes linear in $p_{ji}$, as in `RNA-Sieve`. The
strategies that rebuild DeCovarT for that reference, and the
three-layer law that combines within- and between-donor covariances,
are in the
[tailored vignette](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-strategies);
the model retained for real data is in the
[MLE vignette](theory-DeCovarT-MLE-properties.html#sec-final-choice).

# Cell-type-specific moments when the composition is known {#sec-cts-given-p}

The methods of @sec-methods estimate the composition from known
reference moments. The reverse problem takes the composition
$\{\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\}$ as known, from any of those methods, and
estimates what DeCovarT plugs in: type-level means and covariances, or
the purified profile of each type in each sample. Write the convolution
with explicit latent profiles,

$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}\sim(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)\ \text{independent across }j,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\sum_jp_{ji}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i},
$$ {#eq-latent-convolution}

so that

$$
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}]=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i})=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j ,
$$ {#eq-gaussian-convolution}

which is the released DeCovarT law when the profiles are Gaussian.
Three families use these identities.

- **Type-level gene networks across a cohort.** `CSNet` regresses the
  outer products of bulk residuals on the squared proportions to
  estimate each $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$, then thresholds the correlation
  (@sec-csnet).
- **Sample-level profiles with a covariance across cell types.**
  `Unico` (@sec-unico), and the Bayesian `bMIND` and `EPIC-unmix`
  (@sec-bayes-cts), place a $J\times J$ covariance
  $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g$ across cell types for each gene, independent
  across genes. Their covariance is the transpose of DeCovarT's: it
  couples types within a gene, not genes within a type.
- **Sample-level profiles with a gene–gene covariance.** With Gaussian
  profiles and known moments, the posterior mean of each
  $\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}$ is a Wiener filter; it is derived in the
  [Bayesian Wiener-filter vignette](theory-decovart-bayesian-wiener.html#sec-map-blup).

On the measurement side, these methods need the bulk on a linear scale
(FPKM for `CSNet`). When the bulk is normalised by its own library size,
the known weights act as RNA fractions $\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}$, not as
cell fractions (@sec-measurement).

## Type-level moments given known proportions {#sec-csnet}

`CSNet` inverts the DeCovarT arrow [@suEstimatingCellTypeSpecificGene2024].
DeCovarT takes $(\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\})$ as plug-in and
returns $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$. `CSNet` takes
$\{\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ as known (from CIBERSORT, MuSiC,
or DeCovarT itself) and returns type-level means and a **sparse
correlation network**. The generative identities are the same
convolution as @eq-latent-convolution and @eq-gaussian-convolution, written
across a cohort rather than one sample:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}]
=
\sum_j p_{ji}\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})
=
\sum_j p_{ji}^{2}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j.
$$ {#eq-csnet-moments}

No Gaussian law is required for the moments. Let
$P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J}$ have entries $P_{ij}=p_{ji}$ and
$H\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J}$ have entries $H_{ij}=p_{ji}^{2}$.
Gene-wise ordinary least squares on the linear mean recovers

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{g\cdot}
=
(P^{\top}P)^{-1}P^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}_{g\cdot},
$$ {#eq-csnet-mean}

the bulk analogue of a reference average, now identified from
**compositional contrast across samples** rather than from purified
cells. Centred residuals $z_{gi}=y_{gi}-\sum_j p_{ji}\hat{\mu}_{gj}$
then satisfy the pairwise identity
$z_{gi}z_{g'i}=\sum_j p_{ji}^{2}\Sigma_{gg',j}+\varepsilon_{gg'i}$.
Least squares of the Hadamard products on $H$ estimates each
covariance entry,

$$
\hat{\Sigma}_{gg',j}
=
\bigl[(H^{\top}H)^{-1}H^{\top}(\boldsymbol{z}_{g\cdot}\odot\boldsymbol{z}_{g'\cdot})\bigr]_{j}.
$$ {#eq-csnet-cov}

`CSNet` converts $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j$ to a correlation
$\hat{R}_j$ and applies an element-wise SCAD threshold. That is a
**marginal co-expression** graph, not a Gaussian Markov precision.
The Gaussian convolution log-likelihood in $\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\}$,
which is the natural DeCovarT loss for the same parameters, is neither
convex nor biconvex in those matrices; pairwise least squares is how
`CSNet` avoids that optimisation [@suEstimatingCellTypeSpecificGene2024].

A DeCovarT-native sequel would keep @eq-csnet-mean--@eq-csnet-cov as
the moment step and map $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j$ to a sparse
precision $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ ([network inference](theory-network-inference.html)),
run **after** $\boldsymbol{p}$ has been estimated (@fig-csnet-two-arrows).
A `CSNet` correlation graph is not a DeCovarT precision.

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-csnet-two-arrows
%%| fig-cap: Two inverse problems on the same convolution. DeCovarT estimates p given mu and Sigma. Given p, the MAP / BLUP recovers sample-level purified profiles, and CSNet recovers type-level means and a sparse co-expression network. A precision Omega_j estimated there can be fed back as the DeCovarT plug-in.
%%| filename: fig-csnet-two-arrows
%%| alt: Flowchart. The bulk matrix and plug-in reference moments feed DeCovarT, which estimates p given mu and Sigma. The estimated p and the bulk feed both a MAP, BLUP or Wiener estimate of sample-level purified profiles and CSNet, which estimates type-level means and a sparse correlation R_j. CSNet optionally yields a sparse precision Omega_j that is fed back to DeCovarT as an updated plug-in.

\node[box] (bulk) at (-2.6,0) {Bulk matrix $\boldsymbol{y}$, $i=1,\ldots,N$};

\node[keybox] (deco) at (0,-1.8) {DeCovarT: $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}$ given $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$};
\node[box] (map) at (-4.2,-3.8) {MAP / BLUP / Wiener:\\ $\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}$ given $\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}$, $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[box] (csnet) at (4.2,-3.8) {CSNet: $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$ and sparse $\boldsymbol{R}_j$\\ given $\boldsymbol{y}$, $\boldsymbol{p}$};

\draw[edge] (bulk.north) |- ++(0,0.55) -| ([xshift=12mm]csnet.north);

```

$P$ and $H$ must have full column rank, so $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ has
to **vary** across the $N$ bulks. One sample identifies $\boldsymbol{p}$
given $(\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\})$; it does not identify
$J$ covariance matrices. Rare types with almost constant $p_{ji}$
leave the corresponding column of $H$ weak, which is why `CSNet`
recovers abundant-type co-expression more easily than microglia-scale
weights. The method is a moment estimator: modest errors in the
supplied $\boldsymbol{p}$ are averaged over $N$, whereas DeCovarT's
likelihood for a single column is concentrated in $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$.

| | DeCovarT | MAP / BLUP ([the Wiener filter](theory-decovart-bayesian-wiener.html#eq-map-blup)) | `CSNet` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Known | $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ (reference) | $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$, $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ | $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ (external or DeCovarT) |
| Unknown | $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ | $\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}$ (one sample) | $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$, sparse $R_j$ (cohort) |
| Law | Multivariate Gaussian convolution | Same, posterior of the latents | Moments only; Gaussian optional |
| Second moment | Sparse **precision** $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ as input | Uses $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$, does not re-estimate it | Sparse **correlation** $R_j$ as output |
| Replication | One bulk column is enough | One bulk column | $N\gg J$ bulks with varying $\boldsymbol{p}$ |
| Estimator | Constrained MLE on the ILR chart | Posterior mean / Wiener gain | Gene-wise OLS, then pairwise LS, then SCAD |

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* the reverse problem, with the
composition known and the latent profiles' moments as the target;
moments only.

## Sample-level profiles with a covariance across cell types {#sec-unico}

`Unico` [@chenUnicoUnifiedModelCell2025] takes the proportions as given,
estimated beforehand by a reference-based method, and estimates for each
gene the moments of the latent sample-level profiles, then the profiles
themselves (a samples $\times$ genes $\times$ types tensor). Its model
(equations 3--6, p. 11), in our notation, makes no distributional
assumption:

$$
y_{gi}=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}+e_{gi},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot},
\quad
\operatorname{Cov}\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}=\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}\,e_{gi}=0,
\quad
\operatorname{Var}e_{gi}=\tau_g^{2},
$$ {#eq-unico}

so that $\operatorname{Var}(y_{gi})=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\tau_g^{2}$.

- **Estimator.** A generalised method of moments per gene (equations
  9--12, pp. 13--14): one first-moment condition,
  $y_{gi}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}$, and one
  second-moment condition,
  $(y_{gi}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot})^{2}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}-\tau_g^{2}$,
  per sample, combined with a diagonal weight matrix; that is iterated
  weighted least squares, with non-negative means, a small ridge on
  $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g$ and samples beyond two standard deviations
  dropped (p. 14).
- **Profiles.** The conditional expectation under a Gaussian working
  law (Theorem 1, p. 12),
  $\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{g\cdot,i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}+\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}(y_{gi}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot})/(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\tau_g^{2})$,
  the gene-wise, $J\times J$ analogue of DeCovarT's
  [Wiener filter](theory-decovart-bayesian-wiener.html#sec-map-blup);
  `TCA` is the case $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g=\mathbf{I}$. Distribution-free
  asymptotic tests of covariate effects at the cell-type level are
  offered (Fig. 3b, p. 8).

Critical remarks. $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g$ is identified only from many
bulk samples of varying composition, and the plugged-in proportions are
treated as exact. The bulk variance
$\boldsymbol{p}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}$ is quadratic in
$\boldsymbol{p}$, like DeCovarT's: with
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g=\operatorname{diag}\{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)_{gg}\}_j$ it
is the variance of gene $g$ under DeCovarT. The off-diagonal of
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g$ is what DeCovarT drops by assuming independent
types; the gene–gene couplings are what `Unico` drops (our remark).

*Errors in variables (@sec-eiv):* the reverse problem again, with
two-moment conditions solved by a generalised method of moments.

# Bayesian reference-based deconvolution {#sec-bayesian}

Bayesian methods put priors on the purified profiles, on the
proportions, or on both, and report posterior summaries. They split by
target: sample-level profiles (@sec-bayes-cts) or proportions
(@sec-bayes-prop). A latent-profile Bayesian version of DeCovarT is
derived in the
[Bayesian Wiener-filter vignette](theory-decovart-bayesian-wiener.html).

## Cell-type-specific profiles {#sec-bayes-cts}

(b) `BLADE`: log-normal profiles with a normal-gamma prior, Dirichlet proportions, linear mixing. (c) `BEDwARS`: a cohort-level signature drawn around a noisy reference, Dirichlet proportions, Gaussian residuals.

```{.tikz}
\node[note, right=1mm of x] (nx) {$\mathrm{LN}(m_{gj},\lambda_{gj}^{-1})$};
\node[note, below=2mm of y] (ny) {$\sum_jp_{ji}x_{gj,i}$, log-normal error};

\draw[edge] (p) -- (y); \draw[edge] (x) -- (y); \draw[edge] (ga) -- (y);
\plate{ib}{(p)(x)(y)(ny)(nx)}{$i=1,\ldots,N$}

\end{scope}

\node[stoch] (sj) at (2.0,0) {$\sigma_j$};
```
