```

**`bMIND`** estimates sample-level profiles for proportions estimated
beforehand (by NNLS or `Bisque`)
[@wangBayesianEstimationCelltypespecific2020]. For gene $g$ and
subject $i$,

$$
y_{gi}=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}+e_{gi},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}\sim\mathcal{N}_J(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot},\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g),
\qquad
e_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_g^{2}),
$$ {#eq-bmind}

with $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}\sim\mathcal{N}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{g\cdot},0.5\mathbf{I})$,
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\sim\mathrm{IW}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}_g,50)$ and a
non-informative prior on $\sigma_g^{2}$; the hyperparameters come from
single-cell or single-nucleus summary statistics. Sampling is by MCMC
(`MCMCglmm`), gene by gene. Condition-specific means
$\boldsymbol{\mu}_g^{f}$ give tests of cell-type-specific differential
expression. The authors note that the uncertainty of the estimated
proportions is not propagated.

**`EPIC-unmix`** [@tangCellTypespecificInference2025] keeps the `bMIND` model and adds a second,
empirical-Bayes step: the prior is re-centred on the step-one posterior
means and on their covariance across the target samples, with an
increased number of degrees of freedom
The
target samples are therefore used twice. The bulk enters on the
$\log_2$ scale, so the linear mixing of @eq-bmind is a mixing of
logarithms, which is not the physical sum of cells
($\log\sum_jp_jx_j\neq\sum_jp_j\log x_j$).

**`BLADE`** estimates proportions and sample-level profiles jointly
[@andrade-barbosaBayesianLogNormalDeconvolution2021]:
$y_{gi}=\sum_jp_{ji}x_{gj,i}$ plus a log-normal error, with
$x_{gj,i}\sim\mathrm{LN}(m_{gj},\lambda_{gj}^{-1})$, a normal-gamma prior
on $(m_{gj},\lambda_{gj})$ centred on the log-scale mean and variance of
single-cell data, and $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_1)$.
The mixing is on the linear scale (TPM). Inference is collapsed
variational, with hyperparameters chosen on a grid by likelihood. The
model is diagonal: no covariance across genes or across types.

**`BEDwARS`** treats the reference itself as noisy
[@ghaffariBEDwARSRobustBayesian2023]:
$y_{gi}=\sum_j\mu_{gj}p_{ji}+E_{gi}$, $\log\mu_{gj}\sim\log\mu^{r}_{gj}+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_j^{2}\log\mu^{r}_{gj})$,
$\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha\boldsymbol{p}_0)$, with
half-Cauchy hyperpriors and Metropolis–Hastings chains. The signature is
cohort-level: there is no sample-level profile. As written, the prior
variance $\sigma_j^{2}\log\mu^{r}_{gj}$ is not positive for reference
values at or below one RPKM (our remark).

**`BayesPrism`** places a multinomial likelihood on bulk counts with a
patient-derived single-cell prior and infers proportions and sample-level
profiles jointly [@chuCellTypeGeneExpression2022]. The multinomial is the
Poisson measurement model conditioned on the library size
(@sec-poisson-measurement), so `BayesPrism` is the count-scale member
of this family.

| Method | Bulk scale | Profile prior | Covariance | Proportions | Inference | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bMIND` | linear (not stated) | $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_g,\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g)$ | IW on $J\times J$ $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g$ | fixed | MCMC | sample-level profiles |
| `EPIC-unmix` | $\log_2$ | as `bMIND`, re-centred | IW on $J\times J$, empirical Bayes | fixed | MCMC, two steps | sample-level profiles |
| `BLADE` | linear (TPM) | log-normal, normal-gamma | none | Dirichlet | collapsed VI | proportions, sample-level profiles |
| `BEDwARS` | linear (RPKM) | log-normal around the reference | none | Dirichlet | MH chains | proportions, cohort signature |
| `BayesPrism` | counts | from single cells | none | Dirichlet | Gibbs | proportions, sample-level profiles |

: Bayesian methods for cell-type-specific profiles. None models a $G\times G$ gene–gene covariance. {#tbl-bayes-cts}

The contrast with DeCovarT is the dimension of the covariance. `bMIND`
and `EPIC-unmix` model how **cell types** covary for one gene across
subjects; DeCovarT models how **genes** covary within one cell type. A
separable covariance
$\operatorname{Cov}(\operatorname{vec}\boldsymbol{X}_i)=\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\otimes\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$
for the $G\times J$ matrix of purified profiles would contain both as
special cases (our remark); no reviewed method fits it.

(b) `gnSPADE`: each UMI of a spot draws a type label and then a gene, so the spot counts are multinomial with a probability vector that mixes the type profiles; a gene network enters as a Markov random field on the labels.

Panel b: a fixed alpha generates latent spot transcript fractions q_i; a fixed alpha prime generates latent topic profiles theta_j outside the spot plate; inside a plate over the UMIs of a spot, a latent label z and the topic profiles generate the observed gene w; a fixed gene network and lambda act on the labels.

```

**`DSection`** is the continuous, Gaussian route
[@erkkilaProbabilisticAnalysisGene2010]:
$y_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\sum_jp_{ji}x_{gjh(i)},\lambda_g^{-1}\bigr)$,
with type profiles specific to the condition $h(i)$ of sample $i$,
$x_{gjh}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{gjh},\nu)$,
$\lambda_g\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)$ and
$\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(w_0\boldsymbol{p}_{0i})$ centred on a
prior guess of the proportions, which is needed for identifiability.
Sampling is Gibbs for the profiles and the precision and
Metropolis–Hastings with Dirichlet proposals for the proportions. The
paper offers no log-normal option and recommends linear data. The
variance depends on the gene but not on the proportions.

**`gnSPADE`** [@xieGnSPADEIncorporatingGene2026] is the count route, and it is reference-free. Each UMI
of spot $i$ draws a label $z\sim\mathrm{Mult}(\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i})$ and
then a gene from the profile of that label, so
$\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Mult}(L_i,\sum_jq_{ji}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j})$, with $L_i$ the number of UMIs:
latent Dirichlet allocation with a Markov random field over the labels
built from a protein interaction network. Inference is collapsed Gibbs.

The two differ where the measurement model of @sec-measurement bites.

- **Variance.** In `gnSPADE` the variance is fixed by the mean (the
  multinomial is a Poisson measurement conditioned on the total). In
  `DSection` it is a free gene-wise constant that does not grow with the
  mean, which a UMI measurement contradicts.
- **What the weights are.** `gnSPADE` shares UMIs, so
  the label probabilities are transcript fractions $\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}$;
  converting them to cell fractions needs $S_j$. `DSection` estimates
  whatever its reference scale encodes.
- **Profile variability.** Neither model has a type-level variability of
  profiles across samples beyond the prior of `DSection`; neither has a
  gene–gene covariance. The gene network of `gnSPADE` acts on labels,
  not on expression.

# Semi-reference deconvolution: one unknown component {#sec-semi-reference-methods}

Semi-reference methods have references for $J-1$ types and estimate an
unknown component, usually tumour, together with the proportions. With
one component unknown, the convolution of univariate laws has to be
written explicitly, and its tractability drives the choice of law.

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-dag-semiref
%%| fig-cap: Two semi-reference convolutions of univariate components. (a) `DeMixT`: log-normal components mixed linearly on the raw scale; the density of the sum has no closed form and is integrated numerically. (b) `DeMixNB`: each component is a negative binomial whose mean is already scaled by its proportion; the density of the sum is an exact finite sum.
%%| filename: fig-dag-semiref
%%| alt: Two panels, each inside a plate over samples and genes. Panel a: fixed reference parameters generate latent log-normal normal components N_k; fixed unknown-component parameters generate a latent log-normal tumour component T; with fixed proportions pi_i they generate the observed y_gi through a linear mixture whose density is obtained numerically. Panel b: fixed reference and tumour parameters and a fixed proportion pi_i generate two latent negative binomial components N and T; their sum is the observed y_gi, with an exact finite-sum convolution.
\begin{tikzpicture}
\tikzset{ptitle/.style={font=\bfseries\small, anchor=south west}}
% (a) DeMixT
\begin{scope}
\node[const] (mn) at (0,0) {$\mu_{N_jg},\sigma_{N_jg}$};
\node[const] (mt) at (3.4,0) {$\mu_{Tg},\sigma_{Tg}$};
\node[stoch] (n) at (0,-2.2) {$N_{j,gi}$};
\node[stoch] (t) at (3.4,-2.2) {$T_{gi}$};
\node[const] (pi) at (-2.0,-4.2) {$\boldsymbol{\pi}_{i}$};
\node[obs] (y) at (1.7,-4.2) {$y_{gi}$};
\node[note, left=1mm of n] (nn) {$\log_2$-normal};
\node[note, right=1mm of t] (nt) {$\log_2$-normal};
\node[note, below=2mm of y, align=center] (ny) {$\sum_j\pi_{j,i}N_{j,gi}+(1-\sum_j\pi_{j,i})T_{gi}$\\ density by numerical integration};
\draw[edge] (mn) -- (n); \draw[edge] (mt) -- (t); \draw[edge] (n) -- (y); \draw[edge] (t) -- (y); \draw[edge] (pi) -- (y);
\plate{ia}{(n)(t)(y)(ny)(pi)(nn)(nt)}{samples $i$, genes $g$}
\node[ptitle] at (-2.6,1.0) {(a) DeMixT: log-normal components};
\end{scope}
% (b) DeMixNB
\begin{scope}[xshift=116mm]
\node[const] (mn) at (0,0) {$\mu_{ng},\phi_{ng}$};
\node[const] (mt) at (3.4,0) {$\mu_{tg},\phi_{tg}$};
\node[stoch] (n) at (0,-2.2) {$N_{gi}$};
\node[stoch] (t) at (3.4,-2.2) {$T_{gi}$};
\node[const] (pi) at (1.7,-2.2) {$\pi_{i}$};
\node[obs] (y) at (1.7,-4.2) {$y_{gi}$};
\node[note, left=1mm of n] (nn) {$\mathrm{NB}((1-\pi_i)\mu_{ng},\phi_{ng})$};
\node[note, right=1mm of t] (nt) {$\mathrm{NB}(\pi_i\mu_{tg},\phi_{tg})$};
\node[note, below=2mm of y, align=center] (ny) {$T_{gi}+N_{gi}$\\ exact finite-sum convolution};
\draw[edge] (mn) -- (n); \draw[edge] (mt) -- (t); \draw[edge] (pi) -- (n); \draw[edge] (pi) -- (t); \draw[edge] (n) -- (y); \draw[edge] (t) -- (y);
\plate{ib}{(n)(t)(y)(ny)(pi)(nn)(nt)}{samples $i$, genes $g$}
\node[ptitle] at (-3.4,1.0) {(b) DeMixNB: negative binomial thinning};
\end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

**`DeMix` and `DeMixT`.** `DeMix` mixes a tumour and one normal
component; `DeMixT` adds a second normal component
[@ahnDeMixDeconvolutionMixed2013; @wangTranscriptomeDeconvolutionHeterogeneous2018]:

$$
y_{gi}=\pi_{1,i}N_{1,gi}+\pi_{2,i}N_{2,gi}+(1-\pi_{1,i}-\pi_{2,i})T_{gi},
\qquad
N_{j,gi},T_{gi}\sim\log_2\text{-normal}.
$$ {#eq-demixt}

The mixing is linear on the raw scale, and the density of a sum of
log-normals has no closed form, so `DeMixT` integrates numerically (a
double integral for three components). The normal-component parameters
are plugged in from unmatched normal samples; the proportions and the
tumour parameters are maximised by iterated conditional modes, gene and
sample blocks in parallel. When the two normal means are close, the
likelihood is flat in $(\pi_1,\pi_2)$; a gene-set component-merging step
first estimates the tumour proportion on genes where they agree. Genes
are independent.

**`DeMixNB`** replaces the log-normal by a negative binomial for sparse
counts (miRNA, spatial spots)
[@montierthDeconvolutionSparsecountRNA2025]:
$T_{gi}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\pi_i\mu_{tg},\phi_{tg})$,
$N_{gi}\sim\mathrm{NB}((1-\pi_i)\mu_{ng},\phi_{ng})$ and
$y_{gi}=T_{gi}+N_{gi}$, whose density is the finite sum
$\sum_{z=0}^{y}f_T(z)f_N(y-z)$. The proportions scale the means, not the
dispersions. Read with @sec-measurement, $\mathrm{NB}(\pi\mu,\phi)$ is
the binomial thinning of $\mathrm{NB}(\mu,\phi)$: a Poisson measurement of
a Gamma-distributed rate, with the rates mixed linearly (our remark).
That makes `DeMixNB` the semi-reference model closest to a UMI
measurement. Its $\pi_i$ is a transcript fraction. The method is a
preprint.

**`BayICE`** models $\log(\text{count}+1)$ as Gaussian with mean
$\alpha_g+\sum_jw_{ji}\beta_{gj}+w_{0i}\beta_{g0}$, a convex combination
of type effects plus an unknown-class effect, with spike-and-slab
priors on the type effects (marker selection with a Bayesian false
discovery rate) and a Dirichlet prior on the weights
[@taiBayiceBayesianHierarchicalModel2021]. Inference is Gibbs with
Metropolis–Hastings steps. The mixing is on the log scale, so it is a
mean regression rather than a convolution, and the variances are
gene-wise, not type-specific.

**`ISOpureR`** places a multinomial on the discretised tumour profile,
with probability vector $\alpha_i\boldsymbol{c}_i+\sum_r\omega_{ri}\boldsymbol{x}^{\mathrm{ref}}_r$:
the normal part is a convex combination of individual reference
**samples**, the cancer profile $\boldsymbol{c}_i$ is shrunk towards a
cohort mean by a Dirichlet prior, and the estimate is a MAP by block
coordinate descent [@anghelISOpureRImplementationComputational2015].
Genes are coupled through the multinomial simplex; there is no
overdispersion. Its $\alpha_i$ is a fraction of transcripts.

| | `DeMix`, `DeMixT` | `DeMixNB` | `BayICE` | `ISOpureR` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Component law | $\log_2$-normal | negative binomial | Gaussian on $\log(y+1)$ | multinomial, Dirichlet profiles |
| Mixing scale | raw | counts | log | probabilities |
| Convolution | numerical integration | exact finite sum | none (mean regression) | none (closed by thinning) |
| Inference | ICM, plug-in reference | ICM, L-BFGS-B, restarts | Gibbs and MH | MAP, coordinate descent |
| Genes | independent | independent | conditionally independent | coupled by the simplex |
| Proportion | mixing weight on raw scale | transcript fraction | weight on log scale | transcript fraction |

: Semi-reference methods. The extension of DeCovarT to one unknown component is outlined in the [extensions roadmap](theory-decovart-extensions-roadmap.html#sec-semi-reference). {#tbl-semi-reference}

# Reference-free deconvolution with co-expression structure {#sec-reference-free}

Without a reference, deconvolution is a non-negative matrix
factorisation $\boldsymbol{Y}\approx\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{P}$ with the
columns of $\boldsymbol{P}$ on the simplex. Three recent methods add
gene–gene structure to that factorisation, in three different ways.

**`DSSC`** [@wangDeconvolutionBulkGene2024] fits the bulk and, in addition, the Gram matrices of genes
and of samples
:

$$
\min_{\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{P}\ge 0}
\lVert\boldsymbol{Y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{P}\rVert_F^{2}
+\lambda_1\lVert\boldsymbol{K}_N-\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{P}\rVert_F^{2}
+\lambda_2\lVert\boldsymbol{K}_G-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\rVert_F^{2}
+\lambda_c\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}-\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{Y}_{\mathrm{sc}})\rVert_F^{2},
$$ {#eq-dssc}

where $\boldsymbol{K}_G$ and $\boldsymbol{K}_N$ are similarity kernels
$1/(1+d)$ built from Pearson distances of the **same** bulk, and the last
term optionally pulls the signature towards a transform $\mathcal{T}$ of a single-cell reference.
Multiplicative updates are run without the sum-to-one constraint and the
proportions are normalised afterwards. The gene term matches
$\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}$ to a data similarity; expanded, it
keeps the affinity part of a graph-Laplacian penalty and replaces its
degree term by a quartic term, so it corresponds to no Gaussian Markov
random field (our remark).

**`GSNMF+`** [@liAugmentedGSNMFModel2025] regularises the rows of the signature with a kernel
co-expression graph built on the bulk augmented by single-cell
pseudo-bulks, and pulls marker rows towards the simplex vertices
It states
identifiability conditions (separability, or sufficiently scattered
factors) and that the Frobenius loss is the Gaussian maximum-likelihood
estimate. With a Euclidean distance its graph term would be
$\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{L}_G\boldsymbol{\mu})$, the
log-density of an intrinsic Gaussian Markov random field prior on the
signature; with the cosine distance it uses, the term is quartic.

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-dag-swcam
%%| fig-cap: `swCAM` read as a probabilistic model (our reading, not the paper's). The nuclear-norm penalty on the sample-specific deviations of type $j$ is the MAP of a Gaussian factor model with loadings $\boldsymbol{L}_j$ and sample scores $\boldsymbol{u}_{ij}$, which implies a low-rank gene–gene covariance within each cell type.
%%| filename: fig-dag-swcam
%%| alt: Latent loadings L_j inside a cell-type plate and latent scores u_ij inside a sample plate give the deterministic deviation Delta_i. With the fixed signature mu and fixed proportions p_i, the deviation generates the observed bulk y_i as mu plus Delta_i times p_i plus noise.
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[stoch] (V) at (2,0.8) {$\boldsymbol{L}_j$};
\node[const] (mu) at (4.4,0.8) {$\boldsymbol{\mu}$};
\node[stoch] (u) at (0,-2.3) {$\boldsymbol{u}_{ij}$};
\node[det] (D) at (2,-2.3) {$\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i$};
\node[const] (p) at (4.4,-2.3) {$\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[obs] (y) at (3.2,-4.3) {$\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[note, left=3mm of y] (n1) {$\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{(j)}_i=\boldsymbol{L}_j\boldsymbol{u}_{ij}$};
\node[note, right=3mm of y] (n2) {$(\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i)\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i$};
\draw[edge] (V) -- (D); \draw[edge] (u) -- (D); \draw[edge] (D) -- (y);
\draw[edge] (mu) -- (y); \draw[edge] (p) -- (y);
\plate{types}{(V)}{$j=1,\ldots,J$}
\plate{samples}{(u)(D)(p)(y)(n1)(n2)}{$i=1,\ldots,N$}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

**`swCAM`** estimates sample-specific signatures [@chenSwCAMEstimationSubtypespecific2022].
After convex analysis of mixtures has fixed $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and
$\boldsymbol{P}$, it solves

$$
\min_{\{\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i\}}
\tfrac12\sum_i\lVert\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}-(\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i)\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\rVert_2^{2}
+\lambda\sum_j\lVert\boldsymbol{T}_j\rVert_{*},
$$ {#eq-swcam}

where $\boldsymbol{T}_j$ stacks the deviations of type $j$ over samples
and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_*$ is the nuclear norm. The problem is convex for
fixed $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{P}$ and is solved by ADMM. There is
no co-expression graph. Because
$\lVert\boldsymbol{T}\rVert_*=\min_{\boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{V}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{T}}\tfrac12(\lVert\boldsymbol{U}\rVert_F^{2}+\lVert\boldsymbol{V}\rVert_F^{2})$,
the penalty is the MAP of a Gaussian factor model
(@fig-dag-swcam), which implies a low-rank gene–gene covariance within
each type.

## Three ways gene covariance enters deconvolution {#sec-covariance-flavours}

1. **Graph regularisation of a factorisation.** A co-expression graph
   smooths the signature (`GSNMF+`). Its probabilistic reading is a
   Gaussian Markov random field prior on the signature, exact only for
   a Euclidean, quadratic penalty.
2. **Similarity matching to the bulk itself.** The Gram matrices of the
   factors are fitted to similarities computed from the same data
   (`DSSC`). The data are used twice, and no likelihood is implied.
3. **Covariance in a likelihood, a moment equation or a prior.** The
   gene–gene covariance of each type enters the bulk law: as a plug-in
   in DeCovarT, as moment equations in `DECALS` and `MEAD`, as the
   estimand in `CSNet`, and implicitly as a low-rank factor structure in
   `swCAM`. `bMIND` and `EPIC-unmix` belong here with the transposed
   object, a covariance across cell types.

All three reference-free methods use a squared Frobenius loss, that is
a homoscedastic Gaussian likelihood, and therefore ignore the
mean–variance relationship of counts (@sec-poisson-measurement).

# Synthesis {#sec-synthesis}

| Method | Bulk scale | Bulk variance as a function of $\boldsymbol{p}$ | Gene–gene covariance | Type–type covariance | Reference uncertainty | Error specification (@sec-eiv) | Estimator |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `MuSiC` | relative abundance | quadratic, diagonal | no | no | weights | moments | weighted NNLS |
| `RNA-Sieve` | counts / linear | linear, diagonal | no | no | noisy means | asymptotic (cells) | MLE, Godambe |
| `ReDeconv` | linear (CLTS) | linear, diagonal | no | no | no | asymptotic (cells) | MLE |
| `DWLS` | linear | implied quadratic in the mean | no | no | no | moments | weighted LS |
| `deMixSC` | relative abundance | fitted mean squared plus residual squared | no | no | no | moments | iterated weighted NNLS |
| `RCTD` | counts | Poisson–log-normal | no | no | no | parametric | two-stage MLE |
| `DECALS` | FPKM | quadratic | yes (moments) | no | no | moments, asymptotic (genes) | OLS + sandwich |
| `MEAD` | linear | sandwich over dependent genes | yes (global) | no | yes | moments, asymptotic (genes) | estimating equations |
| DeCovarT | linear | quadratic | yes (plug-in, sparse) | no | bootstrap | parametric | MLE |
| `CSNet` | FPKM | quadratic | yes (estimand) | no | no | moments | moments + thresholding |
| `Unico` | linear | $\boldsymbol{p}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}+\tau_g^{2}$ | no | yes ($J\times J$) | no | moments | generalised method of moments |
| `bMIND`, `EPIC-unmix` | linear / $\log_2$ | $\boldsymbol{p}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}+\sigma_g^{2}$ | no | yes ($J\times J$) | prior | parametric | MCMC |
| `BLADE` | linear | quadratic, log-normal profiles | no | no | prior | parametric | collapsed VI |
| `BEDwARS` | linear | constant | no | no | noisy reference prior | parametric | MH |
| `DSection` | linear | constant | no | no | prior | parametric | Gibbs–MH |
| `DeMixT` | raw | quadratic, log-normal components | no | no | plug-in | parametric | ICM |
| `DeMixNB` | counts | negative binomial | no | no | plug-in | parametric | ICM |
| `swCAM` | linear | constant | low rank (implicit) | no | no | penalised least squares | ADMM |

: Where second-order information enters each method. "Quadratic" and "linear" refer to the weight of a type's variance in the bulk variance ($p_{ji}^{2}$ for a random population profile, $p_{ji}$ for independent cells). {#tbl-synthesis}

## Caveats and defaults {#sec-caveats}

1. **Scale.** Mixing is additive only on a linear scale. Methods that
   mix logarithms (`BayICE`, `EPIC-unmix`) estimate weights of a
   different, non-physical sum.
2. **Cell versus RNA fractions.** Count and topic models (`ISOpureR`,
   `gnSPADE`, `DeMixNB`, `BayesPrism`) and any fit on library-normalised
   bulk return transcript fractions; cell fractions need the cell
   sizes $S_j$ ([RNA-to-cell conversion](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-uncoupling)).
3. **Mean–variance relationship.** A constant residual variance
   (`DSection`, `BEDwARS`, NMF with a Frobenius loss) contradicts the
   Poisson measurement of UMI counts, whose variance grows with the
   mean. Count likelihoods or explicit variance functions respect it
   ([GLM view](theory-DeCovarT-MLE-properties.html#sec-glm)).
4. **Linear or quadratic weights.** Independent cells give a variance
   linear in the proportions (`RNA-Sieve`, `ReDeconv`); a random
   population profile gives a quadratic weight (`MuSiC`, `DECALS`,
   `CSNet`, DeCovarT). Single-cell references with one donor identify
   only the first ([tailored vignette](theory-decovart-single-cell-tailored.html#sec-three-regimes)).
5. **Which covariance.** $G\times G$ within a type (DeCovarT, `DECALS`,
   `CSNet`) and $J\times J$ within a gene (`bMIND`, `EPIC-unmix`, `Unico`)
   answer different questions; neither family fits both.
6. **Data reuse.** Empirical-Bayes re-centring on the target samples
   (`EPIC-unmix`), similarity graphs built from the bulk being
   factorised (`DSSC`, `GSNMF+`) and priors built from the same
   single-cell source as the benchmark bulk (`BLADE` group mode)
   inflate apparent accuracy.
7. **Propagated uncertainty.** Weighted moment estimators (`MuSiC`,
   `DWLS`, `deMixSC`) return point estimates only (@sec-eiv). Few
   methods propagate the uncertainty of the reference (`RNA-Sieve`,
   `MEAD`, DeCovarT's reference bootstrap) or of the proportions into
   downstream profiles (`bMIND` and `Unico` do not).
8. **Identifiability.** Gene-wise scales with perfect markers (`MEAD`),
   collinear reference means (`DeMixT`), and reference-free
   factorisations without separability (`GSNMF+`) all leave the
   proportions unidentified, whatever the sample size.

## Methods to add to this review {#sec-candidates}

Already in the bibliography and worth a section: `BLEND`, probabilistic
deconvolution with automated reference selection
[@huangBLENDProbabilisticCellular2024]; `DeconV`, a Poisson model
aggregated from single cells [@gynterDeconvProbabilisticCellType2023];
`Imply`, personalised reference
profiles [@mengImplyImprovingCelltype2024]; and `DecOT`, an optimal
transport loss [@liuDecotBulkDeconvolutionOptimal2022]. CIBERSORTx
[@newmanDeterminingCellType2019] extends the signature approach to
high-resolution, sample-level profiles.
